edge_cases.gap_description: The node outputs 'presumptively compliant' (5 < 7, no conversation triggering the cooldown), and its cease-communication checklist item asks only about a WRITTEN 1692c(c) notice, so an oral stop-calling demand registers as legally inert. results.derivation_summary: Under § 1692a(6), a 'debt collector' is someone who either (a) uses interstate commerce or the mails in a business whose principal purpose is collecting debts, or (b) regularly collects, directly or indirectly, debts 'owed or due another' — subject to exclusions (A)–(F), including creditors' own employees, affiliated entities, government officers, process servers, nonprofit credit counselors, and persons collecting debts they originated or that were not in default when obtained. A 'creditor' under § 1692a(4) is one who offers or extends credit creating a debt or to whom a debt is owed, excluding those taking assignment of a defaulted debt solely to collect for another; a 'debt' under § 1692a(5) must be a consumer obligation arising from a transaction primarily for personal, family, or household purposes, and a 'consumer' under § 1692a(3) is the natural person allegedly obligated. Henson holds that a company collecting debts it purchased for its own account is not collecting debts 'owed another' and so does not meet that prong (leaving the 'principal purpose' prong unaddressed). Obduskey holds that an entity doing no more than nonjudicial foreclosure/security-interest enforcement is a debt collector only for the limited purpose of § 1692f(6), not the Act's general debt-collector provisions.

edge_cases.gap_description: The node anchors accrual to 'the date of default/breach or last payment' without distinguishing a payment made BEFORE the 2-year period ran (which restarts it under CCP § 360's payment proviso) from one made AFTER it expired (which does not revive a time-barred debt absent a signed written new promise/acknowledgment under CCP § 360). Applied literally, the encoding takes the 2025 payment as the accrual anchor and reports 'not expired,' telling the consumer she has no SOL defense when in fact she has a complete one. Collector-solicited token payments on stale debts are extremely common.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor earning $1,100/week gross is already subject to an active child support wage assignment taking $300/week, and a credit card judgment creditor then serves an earnings withholding order on the same employer. The debtor asks how much the credit card creditor can lawfully take.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node computes the consumer-debt cap purely as a function of disposable earnings and minimum wage, with no account of CCP §§ 706.023/706.031/706.104 priority rules under which a support withholding order takes precedence and the consumer EWO is limited to the residual within the overall cap. Applied as encoded, the rule would tell the debtor (or employer) that the full formula amount may be withheld on top of the support deduction, overstating the lawful consumer garnishment and inviting an unlawful over-withholding. Concurrent support withholding is very common among wage-garnishment debtors.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor paid semimonthly (twice a month) with $1,900 in disposable earnings per pay period wants to know the maximum the judgment creditor can take from each paycheck.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist marks pay period as non-dispositive, but the encoded formula is weekly-only and the § 706.050(b) conversions are not linear multiples of the weekly 48x figure (biweekly 96x, semimonthly 104x, monthly 208x). Most wage earners are paid biweekly, semimonthly, or monthly, so a user applying the weekly 48x figure (or naively doubling it for a semimonthly period) gets a materially wrong dollar cap. Pay period is in fact dispositive to any usable answer, and mislabeling it as non-dispositive is the gap.

edge_cases.scenario: A single parent working at a local minimum wage with roughly $700/week in disposable earnings is told by the formula that about $140/week may be garnished, but that amount leaves her unable to cover rent, food, and childcare for her dependents.
edge_cases.gap_description: The determination states flatly that the lesser prong is the maximum and 'anything withheld beyond that is unlawful,' with no reference to the CCP § 706.051 necessities-of-life exemption (and § 706.052 procedures) under which a low-wage debtor supporting dependents can obtain a claim of exemption reducing or eliminating withholding below the statutory cap. For the large population of near-minimum-wage garnishment debtors, presenting the cap as the operative amount is materially misleading about what will actually and lawfully be taken.

edge_cases.gap_description: The node's checklist never asks what kind of debt/judgment is being enforced. Under CCP § 703.070, property exempt without a claim (the automatic homestead) is subject to enforcement of a support judgment, with the court given discretion over application of the property; federal tax liens (26 U.S.C. § 6334; U.S. v. Rodgers) and consensual/mechanic's liens likewise override the exemption. The determination's bare reference to an 'ordinary money judgment' is not operationalized as a screening fact, so the node will tell a support or tax debtor her equity up to ~$300k-$600k is protected when it is not.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor who moved from Texas to San Diego 14 months ago, and bought his current house 2 years ago, files Chapter 7 and asks how much of his home equity is protected.
edge_cases.gap_description: In bankruptcy — the most common forum where this question arises — 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)'s 730-day domicile rule can force use of the prior state's exemptions entirely, and § 522(p) caps the homestead at roughly $214,000 for equity in property acquired within 1,215 days of filing (and § 522(o) reduces it for fraudulent conversions). California debtors may also elect the § 703.140(b) 'wildcard' scheme instead. The node captures none of these, and would quote a $600,000-ish protection to a recent transplant whose actual protection is far lower or governed by another state's law.

edge_cases.scenario: A homeowner with $200,000 of equity in a county where the exemption exceeds that amount is told the equity is exempt, and then tries to refinance or sell voluntarily while a recorded abstract of judgment sits on title; she also asks what happens to the cash if she sells.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node's determination ('protected from a forced sale') is likely to be read as meaning the judgment lien is neutralized. In fact a judgment lien still attaches to and clouds title under CCP § 697.310 and must be satisfied, released, or avoided (11 U.S.C. § 522(f) or CCP § 697.410) before a voluntary sale or refinance closes, and sale proceeds are exempt only for six months under CCP § 704.720(b) and only if reinvested in a new homestead. Omitting the lien-survival and proceeds-reinvestment rules gives a materially misleading answer to a very common fact pattern.

Under CCP § 703.070, property exempt without a claim (the automatic homestead) is subject to enforcement of a support judgment, with the court given discretion over application of the property; federal tax liens (26 U.S.C. § 6334; U.S. v. The determination's bare reference to an 'ordinary money judgment' is not operationalized as a screening fact, so the node will tell a support or tax debtor her equity up to ~$300k-$600k is protected when it is not.

gaps_found.scenario: A debtor who moved from Texas to San Diego 14 months ago, and bought his current house 2 years ago, files Chapter 7 and asks how much of his home equity is protected.
gaps_found.gap_description: In bankruptcy — the most common forum where this question arises — 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)'s 730-day domicile rule can force use of the prior state's exemptions entirely, and § 522(p) caps the homestead at roughly $214,000 for equity in property acquired within 1,215 days of filing (and § 522(o) reduces it for fraudulent conversions). California debtors may also elect the § 703.140(b) 'wildcard' scheme instead. The node captures none of these, and would quote a $600,000-ish protection to a recent transplant whose actual protection is far lower or governed by another state's law.

gaps_found.scenario: A homeowner with $200,000 of equity in a county where the exemption exceeds that amount is told the equity is exempt, and then tries to refinance or sell voluntarily while a recorded abstract of judgment sits on title; she also asks what happens to the cash if she sells.
gaps_found.gap_description: The node's determination ('protected from a forced sale') is likely to be read as meaning the judgment lien is neutralized. In fact a judgment lien still attaches to and clouds title under CCP § 697.310 and must be satisfied, released, or avoided (11 U.S.C. § 522(f) or CCP § 697.410) before a voluntary sale or refinance closes, and sale proceeds are exempt only for six months under CCP § 704.720(b) and only if reinvested in a new homestead. Omitting the lien-survival and proceeds-reinvestment rules gives a materially misleading answer to a very common fact pattern.

edge_cases.scenario: A judgment debtor is served with a notice of levy on her paid-off 2018 Honda (FMV $9,000). She reads that $7,500 of vehicle equity is exempt, assumes the protection is self-executing, and does nothing; the sheriff sells the car 30 days later and the debtor never filed a claim of exemption within the 10-day window under CCP §§ 703.510–703.520.
edge_cases.gap_description: The rule and checklist address only the substantive exemption amount and the one narrow automatic case (subdivision (d), single-vehicle execution-sale proceeds). For the far more common situation — a levy on the vehicle itself — the exemption is waived unless the debtor files a claim of exemption with the levying officer within 10 days after service of the notice of levy (CCP § 703.520), with the creditor then having 10 days to oppose. Neither the logic nor the checklist contains any timing/procedural fact, so the node tells a debtor '$7,500 is protected' when in practice it is forfeited by inaction. This is a dispositive procedural gap, not a hypertechnical one.

edge_cases.scenario: A married couple is jointly liable on a credit-card judgment. They own two community-property cars, one with $6,000 equity and one with $7,000 equity, and each spouse claims a $7,500 exemption on 'their' vehicle, expecting all $13,000 to be protected.
edge_cases.gap_description: California does not permit spouses to double § 704-series exemptions; under CCP § 703.110 the exemption applies to the community property as a whole and, where both spouses are judgment debtors, is limited to the amount allowable for a single debtor. The node's 'aggregate equity across a debtor's motor vehicles' framing is silent on marital status/community property, and the checklist has no fact about whether the debtor is married, whether the spouse is a co-debtor, or whether the vehicles are community property. A joint-debtor couple would be told roughly $15,000 is protected when only $7,500 is — a large, outcome-determinative error in a very common consumer-judgment posture.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor's only car has an $8,300 FMV and no lien, so $800 of equity exceeds the exemption. The sheriff levies; at the execution sale the highest bid is $7,900, which does not exceed the exemption amount plus costs, and the vehicle is released to the debtor under CCP § 704.800.
edge_cases.gap_description: The logic's flat statement that 'equity above that amount remains reachable' is materially misleading in the very common marginal-equity case. Under CCP § 704.800, if no bid exceeds the amount of the exemption the property is not sold and must be released (with a bar on re-levy for a period), and sale costs are charged against proceeds before the creditor recovers. A debtor with a few hundred or a couple thousand dollars of over-exemption equity would be told the car is subject to sale when as a practical and statutory matter it will usually be released, potentially inducing an unnecessary payment or settlement. No checklist item captures sale-cost/minimum-bid mechanics.

Prop. Code § 41.003; long-standing case law). As encoded, an elderly or deployed owner not physically residing there would be told the exemption does not apply, when in fact it almost certainly still does.

edge_cases.scenario: A homeowner signed a written remodeling contract with a contractor after work had already begun; the contract was signed only by the husband, and the wife did not sign, and there was no 12-day pre-execution disclosure or closing at a title company/attorney's office. edge_cases.gap_description: The exceptions list states 'home-improvement liens contracted in writing' as a flat exception, but Tex. Const. art. XVI § 50(a)(5) and Tex. Prop. Code § 53.254 require the contract to be signed by BOTH spouses, executed before material delivery/work commencement, and (for post-2003 contracts) satisfy the five-day/three-day and location formalities; noncompliance renders the lien void as to the homestead. As encoded, a homeowner with a defective contractor lien would be wrongly told the home can be foreclosed.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor moved to Texas from Illinois 14 months ago, bought a home outright with $400,000 in cash from selling his prior residence, and is now considering Chapter 7. He asks how much of his Texas home equity is protected.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node addresses only § 522(p)'s ~$214,000 cap, but omits 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A)'s 730-day domicile rule: a debtor domiciled in Texas for less than two years must use the exemptions of the state where he was domiciled during the 180 days preceding that 730-day period (or federal exemptions if that state's are unavailable extraterritorially). Telling this debtor he gets Texas's exemption subject to a $214,000 cap is materially wrong — he may be limited to Illinois's ~$15,000 homestead exemption or the federal § 522(d)(1) amount.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor with a $30,000 savings account, $15,000 in a brokerage account, and a $6,000 tax refund — and essentially no furniture, tools, or vehicles of value — asks whether a judgment creditor can seize those assets, reasoning that her total personal property is well under the $50,000/$100,000 cap.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node states the cap and the outside-the-cap categories but never enumerates the closed § 42.002(a) list (home furnishings, provisions, farm/ranch implements, tools and books of trade, clothing, jewelry, two firearms, sporting equipment, vehicles, livestock/pets, unmatured life insurance). Cash, bank deposits, stocks, bonds, cryptocurrency, and tax refunds are NOT exempt in Texas at all, regardless of value. Framing the analysis as 'aggregate value vs. cap' tells a debtor whose assets are all non-listed liquid property that she is protected when she is entirely unprotected — the most common real-world Texas collection target (bank-account garnishment). The checklist references '§ 42.002(a)-listed property' but never asks whether the targeted item is on the list.

edge_cases.gap_description: The override_exceptions_note and checklist limit federal override to 'a federal tax authority (IRS)' and child support. Also, other non-tax federal collection (Treasury offset, FDIC/SBA judgments) preempts Texas exemptions. A student-loan debtor asking whether Texas's unlimited 'current wages' exemption protects his paycheck would be told yes, which is flatly wrong.

edge_cases.scenario: A debtor who moved from Maryland to Texas eight months ago files Chapter 7 and asks how much of her personal property is protected, expecting the $50,000 Texas cap.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node contains no domicile/timing condition. Under 11 U.S.C. § 522(b)(3)(A), a debtor whose domicile was not in Texas for the 730 days before filing must use the exemptions of the state where she was domiciled during the 180 days preceding that period (or federal exemptions if unavailable). Given Texas's very high in-migration and the fact that exemption questions most often arise in bankruptcy, telling a recent transplant she has the generous Texas cap can overstate her protection by tens of thousands of dollars. The checklist should ask about length of Texas domicile and whether the question arises in bankruptcy versus state-court collection.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer is sued in a Texas justice court for a $4,200 credit-card debt and is served when the constable's office mails the citation and petition by certified mail, return receipt requested, which she signs for on March 3. No constable or private process server ever hands her anything in person.
edge_cases.gap_description: The encoded trigger defines the clock's start as 'date of service (delivery by constable or process server),' but Rule 501.2 expressly authorizes justice-court service by registered/certified mail (and by the clerk), which is extremely common in high-volume debt collection. A defendant served by mail is told the rule's dispositive fact is absent or is left unsure when the 14 days began (mailing date vs. signature date), risking a default judgment. The checklist should specify method of service and, for mail service, that the deadline runs from the date of delivery shown on the return receipt.

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer sues a consumer for $8,500 in principal plus contractual interest and fees, but files the case in a county court at law rather than a justice court. The consumer, served on a Tuesday, checks the amount claimed (well under $20,000) and concludes her answer is due 14 days after service.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist treats 'amount claimed of $20,000 or less' as dispositive proof that the justice-court 14-day rule applies, but county and district courts have concurrent jurisdiction over small debt claims and collectors routinely file there. In those courts the answer is due under TRCP 99 by 10:00 a.m. on the Monday next following the expiration of 20 days after service. The rule therefore outputs the wrong deadline whenever amount is used as a proxy for forum; the dispositive fact is which court issued the citation (as shown on the citation's caption), not the dollar amount.

edge_cases.scenario: A defendant served on April 1 does nothing until April 22, then panics and looks up the deadline. No default judgment has yet been signed, and the justice court docket shows nothing filed.
edge_cases.gap_description: The rule reports only the 14-day deadline and is silent on the consequence of missing it. In practice a written answer filed at any time before a default judgment is actually signed defeats default and forces a trial setting, and post-judgment motions to set aside or new-trial motions exist afterward. A user in this very common posture (searching after the deadline passed) would reasonably read the encoded rule as meaning it is too late to answer and abandon a case she could still defend.
